questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: General methods of preparation, properties and reactions
questions.question: Ethanol is converted into chloroethane. Which reagent gives a product that needs no separation from by-products, because all its by-products escape as gases?

solution.key_concept: Thionyl chloride is the preferred reagent for alkyl chlorides because both its by-products are gases.
steps: $C_2H_5OH + SOCl_2 \rightarrow C_2H_5Cl + SO_2\uparrow + HCl\uparrow$
$SO_2$ and $HCl$ both escape as gases, so pure chloroethane is left behind.
solution.why_not_others: $PCl_5$ also forms $POCl_3$, and $PCl_3$ forms $H_3PO_3$, so a separation step is needed. $HCl/ZnCl_2$ forms water, which stays with the product.
solution.common_trap: Choosing $PCl_5$ because it releases $HCl$ gas, while overlooking the non-gaseous $POCl_3$ it also forms.
solution.time_saving_tip: Remember that 'pure alkyl chloride' points to $SOCl_2$.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: General methods of preparation, properties and reactions
questions.question: Ethylmagnesium bromide is treated with propyne, $CH_3C\equiv CH$. Which organic product is formed from the ethyl group of the Grignard reagent?

solution.key_concept: Grignard reagents are destroyed by compounds that have an active hydrogen, such as terminal alkynes, and give the alkane $RH$.
steps: The terminal alkyne carries an acidic $\equiv C-H$ hydrogen.
This hydrogen protonates $C_2H_5MgBr$: $C_2H_5MgBr + CH_3C\equiv CH \rightarrow C_2H_6 + CH_3C\equiv CMgBr$.
The ethyl group therefore becomes ethane.
solution.why_not_others: Pent-2-yne would require C–C coupling, which does not happen here. Butane is a Wurtz-type product. Propane would come from the alkyne, not from the ethyl group.
solution.common_trap: Expecting the two carbon groups to couple, when the Grignard reagent is simply protonated.
solution.time_saving_tip: Grignard reagent plus any active-H compound gives $RH$.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: General methods of preparation, properties and reactions
questions.question: Bromoethane reacts separately with each reagent listed. Which pairing of reagent and major organic product is correct?

solution.key_concept: Ionic and covalent ambident reagents attack through different atoms.
steps: Ionic $KCN$ gives the nitrile, and covalent $AgCN$ gives the isocyanide.
$KNO_2$ gives the alkyl nitrite, and $AgNO_2$ gives the nitroalkane.
Only the pairing $KNO_2$ : ethyl nitrite is correct.
solution.why_not_others: Options 1 and 2 swap the products of $KCN$ and $AgCN$. $AgNO_2$ gives nitroethane, not ethyl nitrite.
solution.common_trap: Writing a nitrile for $AgCN$.
solution.time_saving_tip: The silver salts ($AgCN$, $AgNO_2$) give the 'iso/nitro' products.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: General methods of preparation, properties and reactions
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Addition of $HBr$ to propene in the presence of a peroxide gives 1-bromopropane as the major product.
statements.R: The peroxide effect gives anti-Markovnikov addition with all three hydrogen halides, $HCl$, $HBr$ and $HI$.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: The peroxide (Kharasch) effect is shown only by $HBr$.
steps: With peroxide, $HBr$ adds to propene in the anti-Markovnikov way, giving $CH_3CH_2CH_2Br$. A is true.
$HCl$ and $HI$ do not show the peroxide effect. R is false.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A is true but R is false
solution.why_not_others: R makes an incorrect generalisation, so options 1, 2 and 4 cannot be right.
solution.common_trap: Applying the peroxide effect to $HCl$ or $HI$.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: General methods of preparation, properties and reactions
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: Among the isomeric dichlorobenzenes, the para isomer has the lowest melting point because its symmetrical molecules pack loosely in the crystal.
statements.II: In the Finkelstein reaction, an alkyl chloride is converted into an alkyl iodide by $NaI$ in dry acetone, and the reaction is driven forward by the precipitation of $NaCl$.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Symmetry improves crystal packing, and precipitation drives the Finkelstein reaction.
steps: p-Dichlorobenzene is symmetrical and packs better in the crystal. It therefore melts higher than its o- and m-isomers, so I is incorrect.
$RCl + NaI \xrightarrow{\text{dry acetone}} RI + NaCl\downarrow$. $NaCl$ is insoluble in dry acetone, which drives the reaction forward, so II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: Statement I reverses the actual melting-point trend, so options 1 and 3 fail. Statement II is accurate, so option 2 fails.
solution.common_trap: Assuming symmetry gives looser packing, when it actually gives tighter packing and a higher melting point.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Which carbon–halogen bond has the lowest bond enthalpy?

solution.key_concept: C–X bond length increases and bond enthalpy decreases down the halogen group.
steps: The bond enthalpy order is $C-F > C-Cl > C-Br > C-I$.
Iodine is the largest halogen, so C–I is the longest and weakest bond.
solution.why_not_others: C–F is the strongest bond. C–Cl and C–Br are intermediate.
solution.common_trap: Linking the high electronegativity of fluorine to a weak bond.
solution.time_saving_tip: The longest bond is the weakest bond and gives the most reactive alkyl halide.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Which is the correct order of dipole moments of the methyl halides?

solution.key_concept: Dipole moment depends on both the charge separation and the bond length.
steps: C–F has the largest charge separation, but the bond is very short.
The short bond outweighs the charge effect, so $CH_3F$ falls below $CH_3Cl$.
The order is $CH_3Cl > CH_3F > CH_3Br > CH_3I$.
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 follows electronegativity alone. Option 3 follows bond length alone. Option 4 places $CH_3F$ wrongly below $CH_3Br$.
solution.common_trap: Assuming $CH_3F$ has the highest dipole moment.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a reason for the low reactivity of haloarenes towards nucleophilic substitution?
options: Partial double-bond character of the C–X bond due to resonance
Greater stability of the phenyl cation compared with alkyl carbocations
$sp^2$ hybridisation of the carbon bearing the halogen, which holds the C–X bond more tightly
Repulsion between the electron-rich ring and the approaching nucleophile

solution.key_concept: Four factors make haloarenes unreactive: resonance, $sp^2$ carbon, an unstable phenyl cation and repulsion of the nucleophile.
steps: Resonance, $sp^2$ hybridisation and repulsion of the nucleophile are all genuine reasons.
The phenyl cation is unstable, not stable. Its instability is the reason SN1 is unfavourable.
Option 2 states the opposite of the fact.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Greater stability of the phenyl cation compared with alkyl carbocations
solution.why_not_others: Options 1, 3 and 4 are correct reasons for the low reactivity.
solution.common_trap: Thinking an aromatic cation is stabilised by resonance like a benzylic cation.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_II.label: I
list_II.text: Highest bond enthalpy among C–X bonds

list_II.label: II
list_II.text: Highest dipole moment among the methyl halides

list_II.label: III
list_II.text: Longest C–X bond; most reactive towards substitution

solution.key_concept: Halogen size controls C–X bond length and strength, and resonance affects the C–X bond in haloarenes.
steps: C–I is the longest and weakest bond, so iodides are the most reactive: A-III.
C–F is the strongest C–X bond: B-I.
The C–Cl bond in chlorobenzene has partial double-bond character: C-IV.
$CH_3Cl$ has the highest dipole moment among the methyl halides: D-II.
solution.why_not_others: Option 2 swaps the properties of C–I and C–F. Option 3 gives the highest dipole moment to $CH_3F$. Option 4 assigns resonance to C–I.
solution.common_trap: Matching the highest dipole moment to the fluoride.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the C–X bond are correct?

statements.A: In the C–X bond, carbon carries a partial positive charge and acts as the electrophilic centre.
statements.B: Chlorobenzene has a larger dipole moment than cyclohexyl chloride.
statements.C: An $-NO_2$ group at the para position activates chlorobenzene towards nucleophilic substitution, whereas a meta $-NO_2$ group has little effect.
statements.D: A halogen on a benzene ring is deactivating by its $-I$ effect but ortho/para-directing by its $+R$ effect.
statements.E: The C–Cl bond in chlorobenzene is longer than the C–Cl bond in a chloroalkane.

solution.key_concept: Polarity of the C–X bond and the special nature of the C–X bond in haloarenes.
steps: A is correct because halogen is more electronegative than carbon.
B is incorrect because chlorobenzene has the smaller dipole moment.
C is correct because o/p-$NO_2$ groups activate the ring, while m-$NO_2$ has little effect.
D is correct because the $-I$ effect deactivates the ring and the $+R$ effect directs to o and p positions.
E is incorrect because $sp^2$ carbon and resonance make the haloarene C–Cl bond shorter.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): A, C and D only
solution.why_not_others: Every other combination includes B or E, and both are false.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that a deactivating halogen must be meta-directing.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Bromomethane reacts with hydroxide ion by the SN2 mechanism. Which rate law applies?

solution.key_concept: SN2 is a single concerted step that involves both reactants, so it is second order.
steps: In SN2, the nucleophile and the substrate are both present in the transition state.
Therefore $\text{Rate} = k[RX][Nu^-]$.
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 is the SN1 rate law. Options 2 and 4 do not correspond to either mechanism.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the SN1 and SN2 rate laws.
solution.time_saving_tip: The '2' in SN2 means bimolecular, with two species in the rate law.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Which alkyl bromide undergoes SN1 hydrolysis fastest in aqueous ethanol?

solution.key_concept: SN1 reactivity is controlled by carbocation stability: $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ > CH_3X$.
steps: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane ionises to a tertiary carbocation, the most stable of these options.
The slow ionisation step is therefore fastest for this compound.
solution.why_not_others: 2-Bromobutane forms a secondary cation, 1-bromobutane a primary cation and bromomethane a methyl cation. These are progressively less stable.
solution.common_trap: Using the SN2 order, which would favour bromomethane.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: An optically active tertiary alkyl bromide, whose only chiral centre is the carbon bearing Br, is hydrolysed by the SN1 mechanism. What is the usual stereochemical outcome?
options: Racemisation, usually with some excess of the inverted product
An exactly 50:50 racemic mixture in every case, with no excess of either form

solution.key_concept: SN1 proceeds through a planar carbocation that can be attacked from either face.
steps: Slow ionisation gives a planar carbocation.
The nucleophile can attack from both faces, which leads to racemisation.
The leaving group partly shields one face, so the inverted product is usually in slight excess.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Racemisation, usually with some excess of the inverted product
solution.why_not_others: Complete inversion is characteristic of SN2. Complete retention does not occur. An exactly 50:50 mixture ignores the usual excess of the inverted product.
solution.common_trap: Thinking SN1 always gives 100% racemisation.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Tertiary alkyl halides react faster than primary alkyl halides by the SN2 mechanism.
statements.R: In the SN2 mechanism, the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the leaving group through a pentacoordinate transition state, so bulky groups on the carbon hinder the attack.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Steric hindrance controls SN2 reactivity: $CH_3X > 1^\circ > 2^\circ > 3^\circ$.
steps: Tertiary halides are the most hindered, so they are the slowest in SN2. A is false.
Backside attack through a pentacoordinate transition state is the correct description of SN2. R is true.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A is false but R is true
solution.why_not_others: A is false, so options 1, 2 and 3 are ruled out.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the SN1 and SN2 reactivity orders.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: Benzyl chloride undergoes SN1 reaction readily because the benzylic carbocation is stabilised by resonance.
statements.II: In an SN1 reaction, doubling the concentration of the nucleophile doubles the rate, because the rate depends on both the substrate and the nucleophile.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: The SN1 rate depends only on the substrate, and benzylic or allylic cations are resonance-stabilised.
steps: The benzylic cation is stabilised by resonance, so benzyl chloride is highly reactive in SN1. I is correct.
For SN1, $\text{Rate} = k[RX]$, so changing the nucleophile concentration does not change the rate. II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement II describes SN2 kinetics, so options 1 and 4 fail. Statement I is true, so option 2 fails.
solution.common_trap: Applying second-order kinetics to SN1.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Freon-12, widely used as a refrigerant and aerosol propellant, has which formula?

solution.key_concept: Freon-12 is dichlorodifluoromethane.
steps: Freon-12 is $CCl_2F_2$.
It is used as a refrigerant, an air-conditioner coolant and an aerosol propellant.
solution.why_not_others: $CCl_3F$ and $CF_4$ are different fluorocarbons. $CHClF_2$ is freon R-22, which is made from chloroform.
solution.common_trap: Confusing freon-12 with freon R-22.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Iodoform was once used as an antiseptic. What is its antiseptic action due to?
options: The action of the $CHI_3$ molecule itself
Its high volatility, which displaces air from wounds

solution.key_concept: Iodoform acts as an antiseptic because it releases $I_2$.
steps: Iodoform releases free iodine.
The liberated iodine is responsible for the antiseptic effect, not iodoform itself.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): The liberation of free iodine
solution.why_not_others: The notes state the action is not due to iodoform itself. Hydrogen iodide and volatility are not the cause.
solution.common_trap: Thinking iodoform itself is the antiseptic.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Which compound is the starting material for the manufacture of both phenol and DDT?

solution.key_concept: Uses of haloarenes.
steps: Chlorobenzene gives phenol, for example by Dow's process.
Chlorobenzene is also used to make DDT, p,p'-dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane.
solution.why_not_others: Chloroform is used for freon R-22 and as a solvent. $CCl_4$ is used for refrigerants and as a solvent. p-Dichlorobenzene is a moth repellent.
solution.common_trap: Picking p-dichlorobenzene because the DDT name contains 'dichloro'.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

solution.key_concept: Uses of polyhalogen compounds.
steps: Dichloromethane is a paint remover and metal cleaner: A-II.
Chloroform is used to make freon R-22: B-IV.
Carbon tetrachloride was formerly used in fire extinguishers: C-III.
p-Dichlorobenzene is a moth repellent: D-I.
solution.why_not_others: Option 2 swaps the uses of $CH_2Cl_2$ and $CHCl_3$. Option 3 swaps the uses of $CCl_4$ and p-dichlorobenzene. Option 4 swaps the uses of $CH_2Cl_2$ and $CCl_4$.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the uses of the chloromethanes.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Which of the following statements about polyhalogen compounds are correct?

statements.A: DDT was the first chlorinated organic insecticide and was used against malaria-carrying mosquitoes.
statements.B: Chloroform was once used as a general anaesthetic.
statements.C: Freons are used as refrigerants and aerosol propellants.
statements.D: Iodoform acts as an antiseptic by itself, without releasing any iodine.

solution.key_concept: Uses of polyhalogen compounds.
steps: A is correct: DDT was the first chlorinated organic insecticide and was used against malaria-carrying mosquitoes.
B is correct: chloroform is a former general anaesthetic.
C is correct: freons are refrigerants and aerosol propellants.
D is incorrect: iodoform's antiseptic action comes from liberated iodine.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A, B and C only
solution.why_not_others: Options 2, 3 and 4 all include statement D, which is false.
solution.common_trap: Thinking iodoform itself is the antiseptic.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Environmental effects of chloroform, iodoform, freons and DDT
questions.question: When chloroform is exposed to air and light, it is slowly oxidised to a highly poisonous gas. This gas is

solution.key_concept: In the presence of air and light, chloroform is oxidised to phosgene.
steps: The reaction is $2CHCl_3 + O_2 \xrightarrow{\text{light}} 2COCl_2 + 2HCl$.
$COCl_2$ (phosgene) is highly poisonous.
This is why chloroform must be protected from air and light during storage.
solution.why_not_others: $CCl_4$ is not formed by the oxidation of chloroform. $Cl_2$ is not produced, because the chlorine ends up in $COCl_2$ and $HCl$. $CO$ is not the product, because the carbon is converted to $COCl_2$.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that the poisonous product is $Cl_2$ or $CO$ simply because both are toxic gases.
solution.time_saving_tip: Chloroform plus air and light gives phosgene. Recall the oxidation directly.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Environmental effects of chloroform, iodoform, freons and DDT
questions.question: Chloroform is stored in closed, dark-coloured bottles filled to the brim, and about 1% ethanol is added to it. The ethanol is added
options: to lower the vapour pressure of chloroform so that it does not evaporate
to absorb light and prevent the photochemical oxidation of chloroform
to convert any phosgene formed into harmless ethyl carbonate
to oxidise chloroform completely to $CO_2$ and $HCl$

solution.key_concept: Ethanol acts as a scavenger that converts poisonous phosgene into a harmless compound.
steps: Some phosgene may still form despite the precautions taken during storage.
Phosgene is highly poisonous.
The added ethanol reacts with any phosgene present and converts it into harmless ethyl carbonate.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): to convert any phosgene formed into harmless ethyl carbonate
solution.why_not_others: Light is kept out by the dark-coloured bottle, not by ethanol. Air is excluded by filling the bottle to the brim. Ethanol does not oxidise chloroform, and its purpose is not to control evaporation.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the roles of the precautions: the dark bottle blocks light, filling to the brim removes air, and ethanol destroys phosgene.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Environmental effects of chloroform, iodoform, freons and DDT
questions.question: A single chlorine atom released from a freon in the stratosphere can destroy a very large number of ozone molecules. This is because, in the chain of reactions that destroys ozone, the species that is regenerated is

solution.key_concept: Ozone is destroyed by a chain reaction in which the chlorine radical is regenerated.
steps: In the first step, UV light splits the freon: $CF_2Cl_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} \dot{C}l + \dot{C}F_2Cl$.
The chlorine radical then attacks ozone: $\dot{C}l + O_3 \rightarrow Cl\dot{O} + O_2$.
Next, $Cl\dot{O} + O \rightarrow \dot{C}l + O_2$, which regenerates $\dot{C}l$.
The regenerated $\dot{C}l$ attacks another $O_3$ molecule, so the chain continues.
solution.why_not_others: $Cl\dot{O}$ is an intermediate that is consumed in the chain. $\dot{C}F_2Cl$ is formed only in the initiation step. The oxygen atom is consumed, not regenerated.
solution.common_trap: Choosing $Cl\dot{O}$ because it is a radical that appears during the chain.
solution.time_saving_tip: In a chain reaction, the species that both starts the chain and reappears at the end is the one that is regenerated.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Environmental effects of chloroform, iodoform, freons and DDT
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: DDT gets stored in the fatty tissues of animals and its concentration builds up along food chains.
statements.R: Many species of insects have developed resistance to DDT.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: DDT biomagnifies because it is non-biodegradable and fat-soluble. Insect resistance is a separate problem.
steps: DDT is non-biodegradable and fat-soluble, so it is stored in fatty tissue and biomagnifies. A is true.
Many insects have indeed become resistant to DDT. R is true.
Insect resistance does not explain why DDT accumulates in fat. That is explained by its fat solubility and lack of biodegradability.
Therefore R is not the correct explanation of A.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) is wrong because R does not explain A. Options (3) and (4) are wrong because both statements are true.
solution.common_trap: Linking any two true facts about DDT as cause and effect.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Environmental effects of chloroform, iodoform, freons and DDT
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: Iodoform acts as an antiseptic by virtue of the compound itself, and it was replaced by other formulations mainly because it is non-biodegradable.
statements.II: In the stratosphere, UV light splits $CF_2Cl_2$ to release a fluorine free radical, which then attacks ozone molecules.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Iodoform acts through liberated iodine and was discontinued because of its smell. Freons release chlorine radicals.
steps: The antiseptic action of iodoform is due to liberated iodine, not the compound itself.
Iodoform was replaced mainly because of its objectionable smell, so Statement I is incorrect.
Photolysis of freon follows $CF_2Cl_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} \dot{C}l + \dot{C}F_2Cl$.
The radical released is chlorine, not fluorine, so Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement I gives the wrong mode of action and the wrong reason for discontinuing iodoform. Non-biodegradability is the problem with DDT. Statement II names the wrong radical, so no option that calls either statement correct can be right.
solution.common_trap: Believing that iodoform itself is the antiseptic, and assuming the radical released from a freon could be fluorine.
solution.time_saving_tip: The radical released from a freon always matches the halogen that destroys ozone, which is chlorine.
